body.x: The honest answer is no. If dating means an unsupervised romantic relationship between two people who are not married to each other, mainstream Shia scholarship does not permit it, and good intentions do not change that ruling. But the question underneath the question is usually a fair one: how are two people supposed to choose each other for life if they cannot spend time together first? Islam's answer is not 'marry a stranger'. It is a structured, family-held way of getting to know someone — real meetings, real questions, real time to reflect — that exists precisely so that a decision this large is never made blind.

The boundary in Shia fiqh concerns the relationship itself, not the gathering of information. Before the nikah contract, a man and a woman who could lawfully marry each other are non-mahram to one another: the rules of hijab apply between them, being alone together in seclusion is not permitted, and physical contact is prohibited. Conversation is a more precise matter. Scholars treat purposeful discussion connected to a marriage decision — the questions a proposal genuinely requires — differently from open-ended socialising, but the frame is always purpose and limits, never companionship for its own sake. This is why 'we are just talking' is not, by itself, a category the tradition recognises. Talking inside the structure of a marriage decision is one thing; an unbounded relationship that simply has not been named yet is another, whatever label it travels under. Your own marja's manual gives his ruling in detail, and that ruling governs your case.
Why the tradition insists on structure

It is worth hearing the reasoning rather than treating the rule as an obstacle course. Marriage in Islam is a public contract with witnesses, families, and lifelong consequences, and the tradition wants the decision made with clear eyes, community knowledge, and family support — because those are the very things that hold a marriage up in its hard years. Unstructured dating reverses the order: attachment first, information later, family last of all. Anyone who has watched two people discover a basic incompatibility only after deep attachment had formed has seen the cost of that order, and how rarely the discovery leads anywhere but pain. The supervised route is slower at the beginning and faster at the decision, because the questions that matter get asked while the answers can still change the outcome.

The tradition's own institution for this is the purposeful meeting — sometimes called nazra, the look. A man seriously considering a proposal may meet and speak with the woman, her mahram present, and she with him, for the genuine purpose of deciding about marriage. These meetings are not a formality to be endured; they are the real thing. Both sides are expected to ask about practice, work, money, family life, children, where to live, and the shape of an ordinary week — and to answer honestly, including the unflattering parts. More than one meeting is normal, and leaving a meeting undecided is normal too. Between meetings, further questions can travel through family, and many families now use chaperoned video calls in exactly the same spirit when distance requires it. The principle is constant: the conversation is real, the setting is held, and both families know it is happening.

Meetings at home or in a neutral place with a mahram present, repeated as often as the decision genuinely needs
Written lists of questions exchanged through parents or a trusted intermediary, and answered in writing
Chaperoned video calls for families in different cities or countries, treated with the same seriousness as a sitting-room meeting
Time in family settings — a meal with both families present — where character and manner show themselves naturally
Istikhara and consultation after the information has been gathered, never as a substitute for gathering it

This is where honesty matters most, because it is where modern searches actually live. The mainstream position is that communication should stay within the purpose that makes it permissible: arranging meetings, exchanging the questions and information the decision needs, with family aware that contact is happening. Long nightly conversations that build a private emotional world before any contract drift outside that purpose — and scholars across the spectrum warn against precisely that drift, because it quietly recreates dating under a rishta label. Families draw the practical line at different points, and a couple should follow their own marja's guidance rather than whichever opinion happens to be most convenient. The test many families use is a simple one: could this message be read aloud to both sets of parents without embarrassment? If not, it has left the structure.
Respecting the range without losing the ruling

Real families sit at different points along this road. Some hold every conversation in a sitting room with the tea going cold. Others allow a couple, after the nikah contract but before the wedding celebration, a freedom that surprises the first group — forgetting that after the contract the couple are, in law, husband and wife. Both can be acting in complete good faith. What good faith does not cover is renaming a relationship in order to escape the ruling: calling something an 'understanding', a 'talking stage', or a 'halal relationship' does not change what it is. If you are standing at the start of this, take the encouraging truth with the strict one — the structured route works. Generations have chosen well inside it, and the questions it forces early are exactly the ones that protect a marriage later.

excerpt: Mainstream Shia scholarship does not permit dating as an unsupervised relationship — but it provides a structured, family-held way to genuinely get to know someone before nikah, and that structure is the point.
title: Does Shia Islam allow dating? The honest answer
